title: How images mean — Image Wiki
text:
How images mean
  The gap between what an image shows and what a viewer takes it to mean — and the four things that gap is made of: signs, connotation, codes and modality.

  
    Termsemiotics / how images carry meaning
    Also calledsemiotics, denotation and connotation, visual codes, modality
    Not the same aswhat the picture is of, the artist's intention, whether the image is good
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Denotation and connotationAn image reads only inside a code you already haveModality: how real is it claiming to be?Common mistakes
      
    
  

  Ask for a picture of a doctor and you get a man in a white coat with a stethoscope round his neck. Most doctors are not wearing a stethoscope right now, and plenty never touch one. The stethoscope is not what a doctor is. It is the thing put in the frame so that you will say "doctor".
That object is doing a job, and the job has a name. It is a sign: something standing for something other than itself. Chandler's opening move is that nothing is a sign by nature — a thing becomes one the moment somebody reads it as standing for something else, and it does that by being fitted into a system of conventions the reader already knows.
Two halves are worth separating. The signifier is the physical form on the page: the chrome tubing, the rubber, the earpieces. The signified is what it calls up: medical authority. The link between them is not built into the metal. It is a habit. A word makes this obvious — there is nothing tree-ish about the word "tree", and Saussure's own example was the word open, which means "we are trading" on a shop door and "press this" on a lift button. Pictures hide the same arbitrariness better, which is exactly why they need watching.
This is not theory you have to believe. It is the machinery behind three arguments you will have this week: whether an image "matches" a prompt, whether it is offensive, and whether it is real.
Denotation and connotation
Split what an image means into two layers.
Denotation is the literal content: what is depicted. Panofsky's version is what any viewer, from any culture and any period, would recognise the picture as showing. Two women, a boy, a window, soldiers on a road.
Connotation is everything layered on top: the social, emotional and political associations. Home. Duty. Shame. Fiske puts the difference in nine words — denotation is what is photographed, connotation is how it is photographed.



E. J. Kealey, Women of Britain Say — "Go!", Parliamentary Recruiting Committee, London, May 1915. Public domain.
Denotation first, and only denotation: three people at an open casement, five soldiers with packs and rifles on a road beyond a low wall, a hill with one tree, a ploughed brown field in front.
Now the second layer, which is not in the paint. The window frame puts the women indoors and the men outdoors, so the picture is about leaving. The woman in front holds the other's arm and neither looks at the boy; the boy holds on to her shawl. The ring on the hand resting on that arm tells you she has a husband, and the picture does not show him — his absence is the argument. None of that is depicted. All of it is read.


Connotation has a knob on it. Keep the denoted content identical and change only the form of the signifier, and the second layer moves:



Keep the same
Change only this
What moves




The words on a poster
The typeface
Official, homemade, threatening, nostalgic


The face and the pose
Sharp focus or soft focus
Documentary record or memory


The subject and the light
Colour or black and white
Now, or a long time ago


The scene
Where the frame stops
Isolated, or one of a crowd



Chandler's own examples are the first two. None of them touches what is depicted, and all of them change what is meant.
The load-bearing point: connotation is learned, so it is cultural rather than natural. Barthes takes a pasta advertisement — a bag of shopping, tomatoes, peppers, a red-green-yellow label — and shows that a French viewer reads "Italianicity" from it, while an Italian would barely notice the connotation at all, because the reading depends on a stock of French tourist clichés. Same ink, different meaning, and neither reader is doing anything wrong. When you and a colleague disagree about what an image is "saying", this is very often what has happened.
An image reads only inside a code you already have
In 1972 NASA bolted a plaque to Pioneer 10 in case something intelligent found it. Chandler opens his chapter on codes with Gombrich taking it apart.



The Pioneer 10 plaque, NASA, 1972; designed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake, artwork by Linda Salzman Sagan. Public domain (NASA).
Gombrich's list of what a finder would have to know already. That some lines are outlines and others are shading — nothing in the engraving says which. That the raised right hand means greeting; he notes that a Chinese or Indian viewer could not read that gesture from their own repertoire either. That the arrowhead on the trajectory at the bottom means direction of travel, which requires a species that once had bows and arrows. That the two separate diagrams are separate diagrams.
Every one of those is a convention. A code is a set of them, shared by a group, and a sign only means anything inside one. Photography is no exception: it had to be learned before it became invisible, and the first instant snapshots confused Western viewers who had never seen movement stopped.


Turning a flat rectangle into depth is a skill you finished acquiring so long ago that it now feels like eyesight. Purdue OWL asks the same question from the audience side, and lists the variables worth checking: region, race, age, ethnicity, gender, income, religion. A team spread across a dozen countries holds a dozen slightly different codes, so when two people score one image differently and both can defend it, that is usually where the disagreement lives.
Modality: how real is it claiming to be?
Modality is the reality status an image claims, and the cues by which a viewer judges the claim. Chandler lists them in pairs, high-modality cue first: three-dimensional against flat, detailed against abstract, colour against monochrome, unedited against edited, moving against still. Then content cues: plausible against implausible, familiar against unfamiliar, near in time and place against far.


High modality: a photograph, with everything the lens happened to include
Lower modality: a plate, with nothing in it that was not chosen


The same bird, Phoenicopterus ruber. Left: photograph by Cliff (Arlington, Virginia), 2007, CC BY 2.0. Right: Robert Havell after John James Audubon, American Flamingo, 1838, National Gallery of Art, CC0.
Left says "I was standing there". The evidence is all the stuff nobody chose: a palm trunk sliced off by the frame edge, feathers dropped on mown grass, a wandering ibis, an artificial pond lip.
Right claims nothing of the kind, and tells you so in three places. The bird is bent double because the paper ended, not because flamingos fold like that. Dissections of the bill, tongue and foot float in the top margin at a different scale, in a different technique. The background flock is drawn at a wholly different scale from the foreground bird. This is a specimen record, and it is more accurate than the photograph about the bill.


Modality is not a ranking of media. One frame can raise its own claim on purpose.



Cornelis Norbertus Gijsbrechts, Trompe l'oeil. The Reverse of a Framed Painting, 1668–72, Statens Museum for Kunst, Copenhagen. Public domain.
A painting whose entire subject is a modality claim. There is no scene: the canvas shows the back of a canvas — bare weave, the stretcher, the tack heads, a curling paper label with a number on it. Every high-modality cue Chandler lists is loaded on purpose, and the picture uses them to say "I am not a picture, I am an object in your room."
Look for the same cues doing the same job in a render that wants to pass as a photograph: dust, fingerprints, chromatic fringing, a slightly wrong crop.


Common mistakes

"The meaning is in the image, so there is one right answer." Decodings do not follow from encodings. Hall's three positions are worth having: a reader can share the image's code and accept the reading, share it partly and bend it, or understand it perfectly and reject it. Eco's phrase for the mismatch is aberrant decoding.
"Denotation is neutral; connotation is the biased part." Denotation is only the layer with broader agreement. Barthes ended up arguing the reverse — that the appearance of a plain literal meaning is itself the most powerful connotation, because it makes a reading feel natural.
"An illustration is less honest than a photograph." Different claim, not a weaker one. Purdue OWL's line is that illustrations are selective pictures of reality and that is what makes them useful: a road atlas works because it left out every gas station between New York and Los Angeles.
"I don't have a culture, I just see what's there." The codes you use most are the ones you notice least. Habit hides the work.


Reading an image for meaning, in four passes

Name only what is depicted. Nouns. No adjectives, no story.
List what you added: mood, class, period, who is good. Then ask which learned convention supplied each one.
Ask who would read it differently, and on what — region, age, language, religion, whether they have seen the genre before.
Ask what reality it claims. Photograph, diagram, render, staged photograph? Which cue told you, and would that cue survive a check?
